name: Deslorelin

lead: Deslorelin is a lab-made GnRH agonist mostly sold for animals, such as implants that suppress fertility in dogs and ferrets or trigger ovulation in horses. It shows up on hormone-focused lists because GnRH agonists change LH and sex-hormone output, which in turn shapes puberty-linked growth and looks.

It acts on the pituitary GnRH receptor; continuous exposure suppresses reproductive hormones after an initial surge. In humans it has been studied in research settings, including long-term treatment of children with precocious puberty. No studies address appearance or muscle use.

paras: Its use is veterinary, as a slow-release implant. In hormone-focused discussions it is mentioned as one of several GnRH agonists, with related drugs used in pediatric endocrinology.

It is not approved for general human use. Human safety data come from specialist trials in children and patients, and the veterinary product Ovuplant was withdrawn in the US after fertility-timing problems in mares.

chain: Change in puberty-linked growth and looks
angle.text: Deslorelin is a GnRH agonist that changes LH and sex-hormone output, which is why it appears on hormone lists tied to puberty-linked growth and looks. Pediatric endocrine research exists on related drugs.

lead: Deslorelin is a synthetic gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) superagonist used mainly in veterinary medicine, sold under names such as Suprelorin, Ovuplant and Sucromate Equine [1]. It is used to control reproduction in animals, for example to induce ovulation in mares and as a slow-release implant for reversible contraception in dogs and ferrets [1][2][3].

In humans it has been studied in research settings, including long-term treatment of children with precocious puberty [4]. It is not approved for general human use [1]. No studies have examined it for appearance outcomes.
infobox: Rx-only in the EU; not approved for general human use [1]

paras: Reviews describe deslorelin as widely used for managing reproduction in animals, chiefly to trigger ovulation in mares and to suppress the reproductive axis with implants [5][2]. Studies report reversible long-term suppression of reproductive function in male and female dogs and reversible contraception in male dogs using an implant formulation [3][6].

Deslorelin was among the GnRH agonists used in long-term National Institutes of Health work on precocious puberty, where treated children reached a final height above their pretreatment predicted height but below mid-parental height [4]. Registered trials have also looked at it in boys with precocious puberty, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, short stature and BRCA mutation carriers at high breast cancer risk [7][8][9][10].

As a GnRH agonist, continuous delivery paradoxically suppresses fertility, while its initial effect is a stimulating flare of the pituitary [5]. Like other peptide drugs it is unstable in gastrointestinal fluids, which is why implants or injections are used [11]. Slow-release gel and implant formulations have been tested in cattle and dogs [6][12].

Ovuplant was withdrawn from the US market after mares that did not conceive failed to return to estrus on time; Sucromate Equine was FDA-approved for horses in November 2010 [1]. Development for several human indications was reported discontinued by 2001 [1].

Human studies are limited to GnRH-agonist trials in children with precocious puberty and other endocrine conditions, in which deslorelin was one of the agents used [4][13][7][8][9][10]. No studies found on cosmetic or muscle outcomes.
